title: Velocity gauge POC check-in
summary: Weekly POC sync to review throughput numbers from the 24-hour soak, agree on concurrency targets and batching knobs, and plan a 2-hour stress run with updated queue/backpressure settings. Agreed to bump target concurrency, enable continuous prefix caching for the two top prompt families, and run latency percentiles recording. Action: Redwood to share tuned config and runbook; Keystone to run soak and provide logs; next call in one week or earlier if problems found.
next_steps: Redwood: share tuned pilot config and small runbook (by 2027-02-25)
Keystone: execute 2-hour stress run with concurrency=48 and report latency/95/99 (by 2027-02-26)
Schedule optional mid-week triage if tail latency > 800ms
action_items: Daniel Kim: export config JSON and upload to shared benchmark sheet; due 2027-02-25
Priya Narang: provide sample production prompt families and percent split; due 2027-02-24
Ethan Ross: attach cluster metrics (GPU utilization + queue depth) for the 24h soak; due 2027-02-25
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-23
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Keystone CTO), Ethan Ross (Keystone SRE), Priya Narang (Keystone ML)
transcript_body:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:05] Maya: Yep, sounds good. Thanks, Sofia.
[00:12] Sofia: Cool. Quick agenda — 24 hour soak results, tuning we did overnight, concurrency targets, and plan for a 2 hour stress run. Daniel will walk through numbers.
[00:24] Daniel: Hi all. I pulled the key metrics into the sheet I linked in chat — the bench sheet, uh the link is in the notes. For the main prompt family A we saw steady throughput around 220 rps at concurrency 36, average latency ~310ms, p95 ~640ms, p99 spiked to ~1.1s during a controlled burst.
[00:47] Priya: Wait 220 rps at 36? That seems lower than our earlier internal runs. Are we including cold-starts?
[00:54] Daniel: Good question. The soak excluded cold starts — we pinned warm instances. The variance looks tied to queueing behavior when bursts overlap across prompt families. Our continuous batching window is 12ms right now, which tends to batch short prompts aggressively, but long prompts cause batch fragmentation.
[01:15] Ethan: The GPU utilization averaged 78% but we saw short troughs down to 22% when large prompts serialized, that's when the queue depth jumped. I can share the Grafana dash after the call.
[01:30] Daniel: Right, and that explains the p99 spikes. Also observed KV cache hit rate about 42% for the prefix families we enabled.
[01:40] Maya: Is the KV cache the same as the prefix cache? Are we losing reuse across requests from the same session?
[01:46] Daniel: It's the KV cache — prefix reuse is working but because some requests hit different prompt templates the effective reuse is diluted. We recommended enabling grouped prefix caching for the two high-volume prompt templates. That lifts effective hit-rate to about 68% in our tests.
[02:05] Sofia: So the proposal is bump concurrency target a bit and tighten some of the batching knobs?
[02:11] Daniel: Yes. Two concrete levers: increase max concurrency from 36 to 48 for the pool, and lower the continuous batching window from 12ms to 8ms for short prompt families. Also set queue depth soft-limit to 250 and enable early-fallback routing to the lower-cost variant when queue > 350.
[02:32] Priya: Early fallback — will that change output quality? Our downstream evaluation might be sensitive to model variant shifts.
[02:39] Daniel: Good caveat. We suggest a canary policy: only route 5% of traffic to fallback during the stress run, and annotate those tokens so you can filter them in evaluation. We can also bind the fallback to only non-critical prompt family B.
[02:55] Maya: That sounds reasonable. What about latency SLOs? We need p95 < 700ms ideally.
[03:01] Daniel: With the adjusted settings our dry runs showed p95 ~ 580ms at concurrency 48 with the grouped prefix cache enabled. P99 still hovered around 920ms in the worst microbursts but overall throughput improved to ~280 rps for the main family.
[03:20] Ethan: Did you try changing the batch size cap? We saw longer queues when the runtime insisted on waiting to reach an optimal batch.
[03:27] Daniel: We did — the runtime has dynamic batching heuristics. We lowered the max wait-for-batch from 24ms to 18ms which reduced p95 a bit but slightly dropped throughput. The continuous batching window is the bigger win for short tokens.
[03:44] Priya: Can you explain continuous batching window? I'm fuzzy on the name.
[03:48] Daniel: Sure — it's the sliding window that collects requests before dispatch. Continuous batching stitches requests into in-flight micro-batches without holding for a fixed count. Smaller window => lower add'l latency but less batching efficiency. Bigger window => more tokens per GPU op but higher per-request latency.
[04:05] Maya: Makes sense. Any memory/kv cache tradeoffs when we increase concurrency?
[04:09] Daniel: Yes, increasing concurrency raises working set for KV, so the cache hit rate can fall if we don't pin more memory or increase cache buckets. For this pilot we recommend enabling TTL on low-value prefixes and prioritizing the two high-volume families.
[04:24] Sofia: Ok let's talk about the 2-hour stress run plan. Daniel?
[04:28] Daniel: Run plan: start with baseline config (concurrency=36, window=12ms) for 15 minutes to establish baseline, then flip to tuned config (concurrency=48, window=8ms, grouped-prefix-cache on, batch-wait=18ms) for 110 minutes, drop to 5% fallback when queue >350, and collect p50/p95/p99 along with GPU util, queue depth, and kv hit-rate. Also capture per-prompt-family breakdown.
[04:55] Ethan: We'll need the exact JSON to feed into our infra pipeline.
[04:58] Daniel: I'll upload the config JSON to the shared sheet right after this call.
[05:03] Priya: For the per-prompt breakdown — we'll send you the split percentages this afternoon.
[05:07] Maya: Also request: please enable detailed percentile logging in the runtime for the p99 buckets. Currently we only have 90/95.
[05:15] Daniel: Noted, we'll flip on p99 histogram sampling. Expect a small CPU overhead but negligible to throughput.
[05:22] Sofia: Any blockers on security/compliance for this run?
[05:25] Maya: Nothing new — we have SOC2 in place and Keystone is fine for this pilot. We do want audit logs from the run though.
[05:32] Daniel: Redwood can push the audit logs to your S3 bucket; we'll include minimal obfuscation for user identifiers per your policy.
[05:39] Ethan: Great.
[05:41] Daniel: Quick note on an odd artifact — during the soak we saw intermittent error 503s tied to internal backpressure on the queue manager when queue depth hit the hard limit. That will be mitigated by the fallback policy and by raising soft limit to 250 so we can smooth the curve.
[06:01] Priya: What's the plan for spikes that come from mix changes? For example when prompt family C has a sudden surge.
[06:07] Daniel: We'll use routing policies keyed on prompt family with capacity reservations — keep a small standby capacity slice that warms for family C. If family C surges beyond reserved, the fallback policy kicks in for lower importance flows.
[06:20] Maya: Sounds a bit complex but doable. Is there a recommended dashboard to watch?
[06:24] Daniel: Yes, shared dash: latency percentiles, queue depth histogram, GPU util by shard, KV hit-rate. I'll add an annotation layer for the stress run window.
[06:36] Sofia: Anything else we should adjust before the run?
[06:39] Ethan: One ask — can you add a latency budget for requests that include tool calls? Our tail seems worse when tool invocation happens.
[06:46] Daniel: We can mark tool calls as a separate family and give them slightly lower concurrency or route to dedicated shard to isolate their impact.
[06:54] Priya: That could help.
[06:56] Maya: Ok, so I've got the follow ups: get tuned config, run the stress test, collect logs, then reconvene next week. If we see p99 > 1s we do a mid-week triage. Correct?
[07:06] Sofia: Yes. Also Redwood will share the canary policy and the short runbook for running the tests.
[07:12] Daniel: Uploading config now — link: https://redwood.app/bench/keystone-02 (note: link in chat).
[07:20] Ethan: We grabbed it. One more thing — when you increased concurrency in dry runs, did you see increased variance in gpu utilization across shards?
[07:27] Daniel: Slightly, yes. There's more imbalance when prompt length variance is high. We plan to use dynamic shard balancing in the pilot to reduce hot spots.
[07:35] Priya: Any expected cost delta by bumping concurrency?
[07:39] Sofia: There's a modest increase in GPU vCPU hours but improved throughput reduces per-request cost — net is a small cost per token improvement in our sims. We'll include a short cost delta estimate in the doc.
[07:52] Maya: Ok great. If we find a regression we can always roll back.
[07:56] Daniel: Also note, during the soak we observed an NTP drift on one host that created a few odd timestamps — logs may need alignment. Ethan, you mentioned that earlier, right?
[08:04] Ethan: Yep, I'll reconcile the timestamps before sending.
[08:09] Sofia: Alright, let's summarize action items and owners. Daniel?
[08:13] Daniel: Action list: 1) Daniel — upload tuned config + runbook (by 2027-02-25). 2) Priya — send prompt family splits (by 2027-02-24). 3) Ethan — export cluster metrics and reconcile timestamps (by 2027-02-25). 4) Redwood/Keystone — run 2 hour stress run with annotated traffic and send results (by 2027-02-26).
[08:36] Maya: I'll coordinate the run on our side. Let's tentatively set next check-in on 2027-03-02, same time.
[08:44] Sofia: Works for us. Thanks all.
[08:47] Priya: Thanks.
[08:48] Maya: Thanks, everyone.
[08:50] Daniel: Bye.
[08:52] Sofia: Bye.

Notes / artifacts referenced:
- Config JSON: https://redwood.app/bench/keystone-02
- Benchmark sheet: shared Google sheet (link in chat)
- Grafana dash: /d/keystone/pilot-throughput
